title: Data in scripts
summary: Print values with printf, test with [[ ]] and (( )), check numbers, and keep lists in arrays.

text: printf takes a format first, then the values: %s is a text, %d a whole number, \n the end of the line.
- echo reads its first word as an option when it looks like one (-n, -e). printf never does that with its values.
- Never put data in the format: printf "$x" breaks on a %.
In bash, [[ ]] is the test to write: an empty variable or one with spaces can't break it, and && and || work inside.
- On the right of ==, quotes mean the exact text, no quotes mean a pattern.
- (( )) compares numbers: no $ needed, and > means greater.
(( )) reads a value as an expression. A value like x[$(date)] would run date: input decides what runs.
- So check that it's digits first. =~ matches a regular expression: ^[0-9]+$ is digits, from the start to the end.
A list of arguments lives in an array, not in a string: a string can't keep 'my file' as one word.
- "${opts[@]}" gives each item as its own word. "$@" does the same with the script's arguments; $* glues them together.
- Your own variables in lowercase: UPPERCASE names (PATH, HOME) belong to the environment.
